title: Cleanthes' hymn
hook: Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus praises a reason running through all things

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zeno's lost books, the founder known only through others. Your line was mostly lost. What would you want carried on of you? Day six hundred forty-two.

By day he went to lectures. By night, the story goes, he drew water for gardens to pay for them. He'd been a boxer, he was poor, and his classmates teased him for being slow. They called him the donkey. He said he was happy to be the donkey, since he alone could carry Zeno's load. His name was Cleanthes, and when Zeno died, this slow, stubborn water-carrier became the head of the Stoic school. And unlike his teacher, one thing he wrote survived whole. A song. Today: Cleanthes' hymn.
screen: `A BOXER WHO DREW WATER BY NIGHT.` → `"THE DONKEY" CARRIES ZENO'S LOAD.` → `ONE THING SURVIVED WHOLE.`

segments.voice: First, the survival. Cleanthes wrote many works, and nearly all are lost, like Zeno's. But one poem, the Hymn to Zeus, was copied centuries later by an anthology maker named Stobaeus, and so we have it, about forty lines of Greek verse. It's often called the longest piece of early Stoic writing to survive. Second, what it says. It praises Zeus, the greatest of the gods in Greek religion, but Cleanthes uses that name for something larger: the power that orders the whole universe. In the hymn, the stars and the earth obey him. He steers a common reason, a logos, that runs through all things, mingling with the great lights and the small. Nothing happens apart from him, the poem says, except what bad people do in their own folly. And even then, he knows how to make the crooked straight, and turn disorder into order. Third, the sorrow in it. The hymn grieves that people see this good order and turn away, chasing fame, money, pleasure. It ends asking Zeus to free people from ignorance, so they can live by that common law and praise it. Fourth, what it shows us. The Stoics are sometimes taught as cool logic. Cleanthes reminds us the school started with something like worship. Readers differ on what to make of that. Some hear a personal God. Some hear a poet praising the order of nature. The hymn itself uses both languages at once.
screen: `ONE POEM, SAVED BY STOBAEUS.` · `A COMMON REASON THROUGH ALL THINGS.` · `THE SORROW: PEOPLE TURN AWAY.` · `THE STOICS BEGAN WITH PRAISE.` · then, large: `THE ONE REASON.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Breathe. Let a few of the hymn's pictures pass slowly through your mind, one per breath. The stars moving in order. The earth turning. A single reason running through all of it, through the great lights and the small. Through the person beside you, and through you. Disorder made into order. Don't decide what you believe about it. Just let each picture land, slowly, the way the hymn was meant to be heard. The bell holds the time.
Cleanthes' hymn. A poem by the second head of the Stoic school, praising Zeus as the reason that runs through all things. Today's word.
Your line: the one reason. Once today, when things look like chaos, look for one thread of order in it, however small. Day six hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Students of the Stoics read Cleanthes' Hymn to Zeus, preserved by Stobaeus, as the clearest surviving picture of the early school's reverence for the reason ordering the world.

original.note: Greek: the common reason. In the hymn, Zeus steers a common logos that runs through all things.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn to Zeus is just Greek myth.
what it means: Cleanthes uses Zeus's name for the reason that orders the whole universe, and praises it.

what a scholar hears: the hymn, preserved in Stobaeus's Anthology, is usually counted the longest surviving text of early Stoicism, and its picture of a common logos shaped Stoic theology for centuries.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
